говорить.gloss: to speak, to say, to talk

meanings.en: to speak, to say, to talk
meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to speak, to say, to talk', paired with 'сказать'.
Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'обака'). Common feminine noun meaning 'dog' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Я гуляю с собакой в парке.
examples.trans: I'm walking the dog in the park.

examples.text: Простите, это собака дочери. Я с ней гуляю пока.
examples.trans: Sorry, it's my daughter's dog. I'm walking her for now.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'friend' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: This is Vanya, my childhood friend.

examples.text: Это Паша, мой заместитель. Это Ваня, друг моего детства.
examples.trans: This is Pasha, my deputy. This is Vanya, my childhood friend.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'person; (pl) people' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: There are a lot of people here.
I know the problems of ordinary people.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and, but; so', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'not', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'some, some kind of', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Бред какой-то. Но, с другой стороны, чем я рискую?
examples.trans: What nonsense. But on the other hand, what have I got to lose?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'there', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'cat' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Зачем вам вообще понадобилась эта кошка?
examples.trans: Why did you even need this cat?

examples.text: Ладно, давай сюда кошку, как просил.
examples.trans: All right, hand over the cat here, as I asked.

examples.text: Денис, убери эту кошку отсюда быстро!
examples.trans: Denis, get this cat out of here quickly!

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'екундочка'). Formed with a diminutive/expressive Slavic suffix adding warmth or small scale. Common feminine noun meaning 'one little second, a moment' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Wait, just now, one little second.
Just a second, I'll be right back!
Yes, of course. Wait, just now, one little second.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'on, onto; for', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: The programme is on the website.
He is running for a second term.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Prefix 'на-' marks surface contact, accumulation, or completing a quantity (stem 'брасываться'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to pounce on, attack'.

related.gloss: not to to pounce on (negated infinitive)

examples.text: Секундочку, друг на человека не набрасывается.
examples.trans: Hold on a second, a friend does not attack a person.

examples.text: На кухне никто не хочет набрасываться без причины.
examples.trans: In the kitchen nobody wants to pounce on without a reason.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'to you', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?
And this is for you. A toy car!

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'someday, one day, ever', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Когда-нибудь ты захочешь помириться со своим папой.
examples.trans: Someday you will want to make up with your dad.

examples.text: Вы любили когда-нибудь? Смотрите, мэр стоит на коленях!
examples.trans: Have you ever loved? Look, the mayor is on his knees!

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'лышать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to hear', paired with 'услышать'.

examples.text: Как странно, я ничего об этом не слышал.
examples.trans: How strange, I've heard nothing about it.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'at, by; (у меня) I have', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'they', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Ты преподавай. А они пусть строят свои торговые центры.
examples.trans: You teach. And let them build their shopping centres.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'my own', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: А что я за мэр такой, который держит своё слово?
examples.trans: And what kind of mayor would I be if I kept my word?

examples.text: Ты преподавай. А они пусть строят свои торговые центры.
examples.trans: You teach. And let them build their shopping centres.

examples.text: А они пусть строят свои торговые центры.
examples.trans: And let them build their shopping centres.

meanings.note: International noun in '-ция' (from Latin '-tio'), feminine declension. Common feminine noun meaning 'function, duty' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Well, and what other functions are those?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'well; come on', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Ну что, очкарик? Видишь, ничего не осталось.
examples.trans: Well, four-eyes? See, there's nothing left.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronominal determiner meaning 'what; what a', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Смотрите, какой у нас грязный унитаз!
examples.trans: Look, how dirty our toilet is!

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('other, another, different').

examples.text: Послушайте, а можно в другое место? Здесь плохо пахнет.
examples.trans: Listen, could we go somewhere else? It smells bad in here.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'лушать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to listen', paired with 'послушать'.

examples.text: Слушай, Самсон, я тут подумал. Твой начальник — такой опытный специалист.
examples.trans: Listen, Samson, I've been thinking. Your boss is such an experienced specialist.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'порить'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to argue, to dispute', paired with 'поспорить'.

examples.trans: That's a nightmare, I don't argue.

examples.text: Это кошмар, я не спорю. Но зачем на видео снимать?
examples.trans: That's a nightmare, I don't argue. But why film it on video?

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.text: Мы просто не хотели вас беспокоить. Всё отменим!
examples.trans: We just didn't want to bother you. We'll cancel it all!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'for the sake of', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Work, work. It's all for us.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronominal determiner meaning 'that', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'so that, in order to', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I'm calling to say thank you.
So that there are witnesses, Samson.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'so, then; like that', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: So I shouldn't wait for you?
So I shouldn't wait for you tonight?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I was born and grew up here.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'over, above; at', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: The lamp is above the table.

examples.text: За поведение? Вы смеётесь надо мной?
examples.trans: For my conduct? Are you laughing at me?

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'American' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: The Americans do not need that anyway.

examples.text: На нашей кухне уже есть новый американец.
examples.trans: In our kitchen there is already a new American.

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.text: Конечно, помогу. Кто у вас сейчас начальник?
examples.trans: Of course I'll help. Who's your boss now?

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('big, large').

examples.text: Аракелян просит время. Сумма очень большая.
examples.trans: Arakelyan is asking for more time. The sum is very large.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to know'.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'this, that; it is', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: And this is for you. A toy car!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'he; it', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'what', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'казать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to say, to tell', paired with 'говорить'.

examples.trans: Tell us, when will your programme be out?
